subsection: 1. Classification, nutritional significance and contribution to the diet

notes.b: Vegetables are grouped by the part of the plant that is eaten, and this largely determines which nutrients they supply. Learn the nine classes, an example of each and one nutritional note for each.
points: Roots (carrots, turnips, beetroot, parsnips) are the plant's storage organs, so they supply starch and sugars. Orange varieties such as carrots are rich in beta-carotene (the orange pigment the body turns into vitamin A).
Bulbs (onions, leeks) are layered leaf bases that store sugar, which is why they give flavour. Onions contain small amounts of sugar.
Tubers (potatoes) are swollen underground stems that store starch. Potatoes also supply some vitamin C.
Leafy greens (cabbage, spinach, lettuce, kale) are good sources of folate (a B vitamin), calcium and non-haem iron (the plant form of iron), plus vitamin C.
Flowers (broccoli, cauliflower) are the edible flower buds, and they supply vitamin C and folate.

Pulses (peas, beans, lentils, chickpeas) are the seeds of leguminous plants (plants that carry their seeds in pods). They are richer in protein and fibre than any other vegetable, and examiners often call them pulse vegetables.
Stems (asparagus, celery) are edible shoots and stalks. They have a high water content and little energy.
Fruit vegetables (tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers) are the fruit or seed-bearing part of the plant but are eaten as a savoury vegetable. Tomatoes and peppers supply vitamin C.
Fungi (mushrooms) are not plants. They are a source of riboflavin (B2) and niacin, which are B vitamins.
notes.tip: Potatoes are tubers, not roots. Onions and leeks are bulbs. Put tomatoes, peppers and cucumbers under fruit vegetables, as the marking schemes do. Never call mushrooms a plant class. Examiners give a mark per class plus a mark per example.

notes.b: Fruit is grouped by its structure and type, and each group has a typical nutritional strength. Know the six classes, examples of each and what each is best for.
points: Citrus fruit (oranges, lemons, limes, grapefruit, mandarins) is among the richest dietary sources of vitamin C.
Soft and berry fruit (strawberries, raspberries, blackcurrants, blueberries, blackberries, grapes) are small and juicy. Blackcurrants and strawberries are high in vitamin C.
Stone fruit (plums, peaches, nectarines, cherries, apricots) has one large stone enclosing the seed. Apricots are rich in pro-vitamin A (beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A).
Pome or hard fruit (apples, pears) is fleshy fruit with a core containing the seeds. The skin and flesh of apples supply pectin (a soluble fibre) and fibre.
Dried fruit (raisins, sultanas, currants, prunes, dates, figs, apricots) is concentrated in sugar, energy and fibre because the water has been removed.
Other, tropical or exotic fruit (bananas, kiwi, pineapple, mango, melon, rhubarb): kiwi fruit is a valuable source of vitamin C, and yellow, orange and red fruit such as mango supply pro-vitamin A.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to classify fruit and give examples of each class, or to name two or three fruits in a given class. Avocado is a fat-containing exception, so mention it only for its fat.

notes.b: Nutritive value means what is actually in the food. For vegetables, work through the nutrients in turn: protein, fat, carbohydrate, vitamins, minerals and water, then what each does in the body.
points: Protein: vegetables contain small amounts, a few per cent of their weight (marking schemes give about 1 to 8 per cent), and it is mainly low-biological-value (LBV) protein. Pulses are the best vegetable source, and soya beans supply high-biological-value (HBV) protein.
Fat: vegetables are generally very low in fat, so they are low in energy. Olives, avocados and soya beans are the exceptions and supply mainly unsaturated fat. Vegetables contain no cholesterol.
Carbohydrate: vegetables provide fibre (non-starch polysaccharides, or NSP), starch in potatoes, root vegetables and pulses, and small amounts of sugar in carrots and onions.

Fibre adds bulk to the stool and stimulates peristalsis (the wave-like muscle movements that push food through the gut), so it helps prevent constipation. It may reduce the risk of bowel disease, such as diverticular disease and cancer of the bowel, and it promotes fullness.
Beta-carotene (pro-vitamin A): dark green, orange, yellow and red vegetables supply it, and the body converts it to vitamin A. Vitamin C comes from green vegetables, peppers, tomatoes and potatoes.

B vitamins and others: pulses and green vegetables supply thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2) and B6, and leafy greens supply folate. Green vegetables also supply vitamin K. Vitamins A, C and E act as antioxidants.
Minerals: non-haem iron (dark green vegetables and pulses), calcium (green leafy vegetables), potassium and magnesium, with traces of zinc and iodine.
Water: vegetables are roughly 70 to 95 per cent water, which contributes to hydration and gives them a low energy density (little energy for their weight).
notes.tip: This is the 'nutritional significance of vegetables' answer, a long Higher Level question. Go through each nutrient and give the role of each in the body, such as growth, energy, bowel, immune system, nerves, muscle, blood, bones and hydration. Vegetables have LBV protein and only soya approaches HBV, so never say all plant protein is HBV. Beta-carotene is pro-vitamin A, not vitamin A. Vegetables do not contain vitamin B12 or much vitamin D.

notes.b: Fruit is mainly sugar, fibre and water, with a few important vitamins. It has almost no protein or fat, which sets it apart from many other foods.
points: Carbohydrate: all fruit contains natural sugars (glucose, fructose and sucrose), which provide energy and sweetness.
Underripe fruit such as bananas contains starch, which turns into sugar as the fruit ripens, so ripe fruit tastes sweeter.
Fibre: cellulose in the cell walls is an insoluble fibre, and pectin is a soluble fibre found in the cell walls of fruit.
Fruit contains almost no protein and virtually no fat. Avocados are the exception, supplying mainly unsaturated fat.
Vitamin C: citrus fruit, kiwi fruit, blackcurrants and strawberries are among the best sources. Blackcurrants and kiwi fruit are among the very best.
Yellow, orange and red fruit provide pro-vitamin A (beta-carotene), which the body converts to vitamin A.
Minerals: bananas are a useful source of potassium, while fruit contains only small amounts of calcium and iron.
Fruit has a high water content, which contributes to hydration.
notes.tip: 'Fruit and vegetables have no fibre' is a false true/false statement, because both supply fibre. Fill-in-the-gap questions often ask for citrus fruit as a source of vitamin C.

notes.h: Dietetic value and contribution to the diet
notes.b: Dietetic value means which diets or conditions a food suits, not what is in it. Fruit and vegetables suit many diets, but they also have limits.
points: Low energy density, high fibre and high water content make fruit and vegetables filling, so they suit weight control and low-calorie diets.
They are low in fat, with little of it saturated, and vegetables contain no cholesterol, and their fibre helps too, so they suit low-fat, low-cholesterol and heart-healthy diets.
Soya beans and pulses provide protein for vegetarian and vegan diets, and vegetables add iron and folate to those diets.
The antioxidant vitamins A, C and E help protect cells against damage. Vitamin C also supports the immune system and iron absorption, and fibre supports bowel health.
Limits: vegetables do not provide vitamin B12 and are poor in vitamin D, so they cannot meet all nutritional needs alone.
Dried fruit, fruit juice and fruit canned in syrup are high in sugar, so people controlling blood glucose or weight should watch the amount.
Practical value: fruit and vegetables are versatile, available all year (frozen, canned, dried), economical when in season and quick to prepare.
notes.tip: Keep nutritive value (what is in the food) separate from dietetic value (who benefits), because the exam asks for both. Good answers cover low-calorie, low-cholesterol, high-fibre, vegetarian, versatile and economical, and then name the limits: no vitamin B12, little vitamin D, and sugar in dried and syrup-canned fruit. A question on four reasons to include fruit and vegetables is answered from here.

notes.b: Irish guidelines set a target number of servings, and surveys show many people fall short. You need both the guidance and the skill of commenting on consumption data.
points: The Department of Health's Healthy Food for Life guidelines and Food Pyramid (2016) make vegetables, salad and fruit the base shelf, the largest shelf of the Pyramid, with 5 to 7 servings a day for adults. HSE and safefood publish the Pyramid material.
Marking schemes phrase the target as 'five portions plus', so you may quote it in that form.
Fruit juice, if drunk, should be unsweetened and counts as at most one serving a day. Whole fruit is better because it gives fibre that juice lacks.
Foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt sit on the small top shelf of the Pyramid.
Surveys of Irish people show many do not reach the recommended number of servings.

To comment on a chart, state the share eating none, the share reaching five, and the difference between groups such as adults and children or men and women. Write in full sentences that use the chart's figures.
notes.tip: Exams give a bar chart or table of consumption against the guidelines (five portions plus). Say who is under or over, give reasons and suggest changes. Reasons women often eat more than men: they are more health and weight conscious, aware of the nutritional benefits, and use salads in low-calorie diets. Present these as reasons, not as a fact about all women.

notes.b: Exams ask you to suggest ways a named group, such as children, teenagers or men, could eat more fruit and vegetables. Each idea works by hiding, adding or swapping in produce, so give the way and a short reason.
points: Add vegetables to soups, stews, sauces, curries and Bolognese, and grate or blend them into dishes so that fussy eaters hardly notice them.
Add fruit to breakfast cereals, yoghurt, baking and desserts, or use fruit salads as fillings.
Make smoothies and fresh juices, and add greens such as spinach to smoothies, which adds vitamins without a strong taste.
Use spiralised vegetable noodles or cauliflower rice in place of some starchy carbohydrate foods.
Serve vegetarian main courses, and use vegetables in stir-fries and as toppings on pizza.
For children, cut vegetables into shapes with cutters to make them fun, and try new vegetables and cooking methods.
Pack cherry tomatoes, carrot sticks and fruit pieces for lunch boxes and snacks, and choose fruit instead of sweet snacks.
Grow vegetables at home, so that people are more willing to eat what they have grown.
notes.tip: Examiners usually want two to four ways, each with a short reason it works for the named group. Fill-in-the-gap items also test in-season produce, which is economical when in season.

keyTerms.definition: The edible seeds of leguminous plants, such as peas, beans and lentils, which are richer in protein and fibre than other vegetables.
Beta-carotene, a pigment in orange, yellow, red and dark green produce that the body converts into vitamin A.
A plant carbohydrate that the body cannot digest, forming dietary fibre in the cell walls of fruit and vegetables.
Protein that lacks one or more essential amino acids in the proportions the body needs, as found in most vegetables.
A swollen underground stem that stores starch, such as the potato.
A fleshy fruit with a central core containing the seeds, such as the apple or pear.
A fruit with a single hard stone enclosing the seed, such as the plum, cherry or apricot.
A nutrient or compound that protects cells against damage caused by free radicals, such as vitamins A, C and E.

factCards.term: Two reasons vegetables suit weight-control diets
factCards.definition: They are low in energy and fat, and their fibre and water content increase fullness.

factCards.term: Daily fruit and vegetable target in Irish guidance
factCards.definition: At least five portions a day, under the Department of Health healthy-eating guidelines.

questions.prompt: Name one vegetable from each of three different classes and give one nutrient supplied by each.
questions.model: Any three classes with an example and a nutrient, for example: roots, carrots, beta-carotene; leafy greens, spinach, folate or iron; pulses, peas, protein and fibre; bulbs, onions, flavour and small amounts of sugar; tubers, potatoes, starch and vitamin C; flowers, broccoli, vitamin C.

questions.prompt: Assess the contribution of fruit and vegetables to a healthy diet, referring to their nutritive value, the ways they can be included in meals, and current healthy-eating guidance.
questions.model: Nutritive value: fruit supplies sugars, fibre (cellulose and pectin), vitamin C and pro-vitamin A, with little protein or fat and small amounts of minerals; vegetables supply small amounts of mainly low-biological-value protein, pulses and soya as richer sources, very little fat, fibre, starch in potatoes, roots and pulses, beta-carotene, vitamin C, B vitamins, folate, vitamin K, non-haem iron and calcium. Contribution: low energy and fat with high fibre and water supports weight control; no cholesterol and little saturated fat supports heart health; antioxidant vitamins protect cells; pulses and soya support vegetarian diets. Limitations: no vitamin B12 and poor in vitamin D. Ways to include: soups, stews, sauces, smoothies, juices, stir-fries, fruit with cereals and yoghurt, vegetable noodles or cauliflower rice in place of starch, vegetarian main courses, lunch-box snacks. Guidance: Department of Health healthy-eating guidelines and Food Pyramid recommend at least five portions a day, with fruit and vegetables on the lower shelves of the pyramid, which are eaten most often.
